headline: Isaias remnants soak Connecticut as coastal flooding statement covers Fairfield County
dek: Several Connecticut communities recorded more than 2 inches of rain Sunday, while the National Weather Service warned of minor shoreline flooding and another wet commute Monday.
body: Remnants of Hurricane Isaias brought a soaking Sunday to Connecticut, with several communities reporting more than 2 inches of rain and additional showers expected Monday morning. The rain was not accompanied by immediate reports of widespread flooding or storm damage, but the National Weather Service issued a coastal-flood statement for southern Fairfield County as high tide approached.

The [National Weather Service statement](https://forecast.weather.gov/wwamap/wwatxtget.php?cwa=OKX&wwa=coastal+flood+statement), issued early Monday, covered 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. and warned of up to one-half foot of inundation above ground level in vulnerable areas near the waterfront and shoreline. The agency said some water could reach low-lying roads and property, and advised people not to drive through flooded roadways. It also said another round of minor coastal flooding was possible with Tuesday morning’s high tide.

Rainfall reports collected by the Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network and compiled by [CT Insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/weather/article/ct-weather-rainfall-totals-hurricane-isaias-22472950.php) showed the heaviest early totals in central and eastern parts of the state. Higganum and Moodus each recorded 2.35 inches by 7 a.m., while East Lyme and Prospect each topped 2.3 inches. Reports also included 2.25 inches in Colchester, 2.19 inches in Mystic, 2.17 inches in Fairfield and more than 2 inches in places including Wallingford Center, Stratford, Willimantic and West Hartford. The readings were taken at different times and can change as observers submit or correct reports, so they are not a single official statewide storm total.

The rain was expected to matter most during Monday’s morning travel period. CT Insider meteorologist Dan Amarante reported that showers could reduce visibility and leave roads wet, with another three-quarters of an inch to an inch possible in parts of Connecticut and locally higher amounts if a heavier band formed. Temporary ponding remained possible in poor-drainage areas, although the forecast called for the system to keep moving rather than stall over the state, limiting the likelihood of a more substantial, widespread flooding event.

Isaias reached the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 hurricane Friday before weakening as it moved north. The [Associated Press reported](https://apnews.com/article/hurricane-isaias-flooding-power-outages-e1fc35b66ff106211e287dc88b6a8d1a) that the storm’s remnants produced flooding in western North Carolina and that at least four deaths had been linked to the hurricane. That broader history helps explain why forecasters were watching the storm’s moisture, but it does not mean Connecticut experienced hurricane conditions. The local concern was the combination of saturated ground, continued rain, high tide and vulnerable drainage or shoreline locations.

Conditions were expected to improve gradually Monday afternoon as the steadiest rain moved away. CT Insider’s regional forecast called for Tuesday to be drier with a mix of clouds and sun, followed by more breaks Wednesday and cooler temperatures Thursday. Along the shoreline, Monday highs were forecast in the upper 60s to low 70s, with breezy conditions and possible gusts near 20 to 30 mph; inland areas were expected to follow a similar rain-to-showers pattern.

Forecasters were also monitoring a separate coastal low expected to develop later in the week. The [National Weather Service Boston/Norton forecast discussion](https://forecast.weather.gov/product.php?format=CI&glossary=1&highlight=off&issuedby=BOX&product=AFD&site=NWS&version=15) said model guidance supported the possibility of strong gusts, rain and coastal impacts, but emphasized that the storm’s track and strength remained uncertain. For Connecticut residents, the practical sequence is clear even as the longer-range details change: monitor local alerts, allow extra time on wet roads, avoid flooded pavement and use town or county guidance for any street or shoreline closure.

The immediate event therefore looks more like a prolonged, uneven rain and coastal-water problem than a repeat of a landfalling hurricane. Communities that received the highest totals may see localized drainage issues, while exposed Fairfield County shorelines face the greatest tide-related concern. Officials had not reported a broad emergency as of Monday morning, but the combination of more rain and a second high-tide cycle meant conditions could still change in specific neighborhoods before the weather settled.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Isaias remnants bring rain and minor coastal flooding to Connecticut
seoDescription: Connecticut communities reported more than 2 inches of rain from Isaias remnants as the National Weather Service warned of minor Fairfield County coastal flooding.
